headline: Nvidia's Huang resigns; Trump says no Iran deal needed
briefing: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive on Thursday and the stock opened about 14% lower before recovering much of the loss, while the wider market held steady. President Trump said the U.S. no longer needs a deal with Iran and pulled Vice-President Vance off the talks, which nudged oil higher. In Toronto, federal and Ontario ministers and the union Unifor are meeting Stellantis over its sale of the idled Brampton assembly plant.

keyDates.why: Ontario councils and the appointed regional chairs begin their four-year term, and Israel's security cabinet is due to meet again after ordering readiness for a possible Iran strike.

keyDates.why: The chipmaker is due to report earnings, its first under interim CEO Colette Kress after Jensen Huang's resignation.

keyDates.why: Both central banks decide the same day; oil prices and inflation keep further hikes on the table.

stories.backstory: Huang co-founded Nvidia and has run it since 1993, building it into the main supplier of the chips used to train artificial intelligence (AI) systems and one of the world's most valuable companies. Earlier this week, reports said the company had opened an internal investigation into whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort through a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly passed information to Beijing. Huang told staff in a company email that he had been unfaithful in his marriage. The stock had already slipped on that first report before Wednesday's news.
stories.headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns; finance chief Colette Kress takes over for now
stories.impact: Most Canadian pension plans, index funds and RRSP or TFSA portfolios that track U.S. stocks hold Nvidia, so its swings show up in retirement savings here. Thursday's quick rebound in the wider market limited the damage, but the company's next results and its CEO search could bring more volatility.
stories.now: Nvidia announced Thursday morning that Huang has left all his roles, and a spokesperson said he will not work with the company in any capacity. Chief financial officer Colette Kress becomes interim CEO, former Synopsys chief Harvey Jones becomes the company's first board chair, and the board has started a search for a permanent CEO that will look at internal and external candidates. The shares fell about 14% at the open to roughly US$148.80, from Wednesday's close of US$173.73, then pared the loss to about 5% by late morning. The wider market shrugged it off: at about 11:45 a.m. ET the Dow was up 0.3% and the S&P 500 and Nasdaq were each up 0.2%. The departure follows reports of extramarital relationships, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly believe was working for China.

The spying allegation also raises national-security questions in Washington, which controls what chips the company may sell to China.

stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Iran choked traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, route for about a fifth of the world's oil. A June peace memorandum briefly reopened it but collapsed in July, and the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping. Qatar gave Iran a new draft deal on Oct. 25. Trump has said the war will end soon, one way or the other.
stories.headline: Trump says U.S. needs no deal with Iran and pulls Vance off the talks
stories.impact: Lower crude usually reaches GTA gas pumps within days, and this month's drop has eased fuel and delivery costs. With Trump stepping back from talks and Israel raising readiness, an Israeli strike or new attacks on shipping could quickly reverse that.
stories.now: Trump posted on Truth Social on Thursday that the U.S. does not need a deal with Iran, pointing to American control over the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's frozen funds, and directed Vance to focus on fraud and crime at home instead. The post followed a Wall Street Journal report that Vance was weighing a face-to-face meeting with Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council; Rezaei denied talks were planned. Israeli broadcaster KAN reported late Wednesday that the security cabinet told the military to step up preparations for a possible attack on Iran, and the cabinet is due to meet again Sunday. Iranian forces said they stopped two tankers in the strait on Wednesday night. Brent crude was up about 1.1% at US$93.73 a barrel on Thursday and U.S. benchmark WTI (West Texas Intermediate) up 0.3% at US$86.76; Brent is still down about 20% this month.

stories.headline: Ottawa, Ontario and Unifor confront Stellantis over sale of Brampton plant
stories.summary: Federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is meeting Stellantis, the union Unifor and an Ontario minister in Toronto on Thursday, three days after the automaker said it will sell its idled Brampton assembly plant to armoured-vehicle maker Roshel.
stories.now: Joly called Thursday's meeting in Toronto with Stellantis, Unifor and Ontario's government; reports name Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli as the provincial representative. Stellantis said Monday it will sell the Brampton plant to Canadian defence firm Roshel for an undisclosed price, and that 700 to 1,000 laid-off employees could have a chance to work for the new owner; CTV reports about 2,200 workers are on layoff, and Roshel's chief executive said his company will not take responsibility for rehiring all of them. Prime Minister Carney called the sale a betrayal of the workers and said Canada will fully enforce its rights under its funding agreements. A CTV News report on Thursday said the government knew of the deal beforehand; Carney said he had been told of some aspects of the plan but that the company still broke its commitments. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has called for Joly to be fired, and her office says she had no part in negotiating the sale.
stories.backstory: The Brampton plant built Dodge and Chrysler cars and has been idle for about three years while workers stayed on paid layoff. In May 2022 Ottawa agreed to give Stellantis $529 million to retool its Brampton and Windsor plants, and the company had planned to build the Jeep Compass in Brampton. In October 2025 it moved that vehicle to Illinois as U.S. tariffs on Canadian-made cars took hold. Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with Roshel in September, Unifor's contract expired Sept. 20, and the union declared an impasse over the plant's future.

stories.why: The sale ends hopes that a major GTA auto plant would restart vehicle production, and it tests whether governments can enforce the conditions attached to public subsidies. It also shows how U.S. tariffs are pulling auto investment out of Ontario.
stories.impact: Thousands of Peel Region families depend on the plant and its parts suppliers, and most laid-off workers have no guarantee of a job with the new owner. Taxpayers have a stake too: Ottawa says it will seek its money back if Stellantis does not meet its obligations.

stories.backstory: U.S.-mediated efforts to end the war stalled for months while Washington focused on Iran. Rubio said in May that the effort had stagnated. Europe has repeatedly asked to be included in any deal affecting its own security.
stories.headline: U.S. envoys meet Putin in Moscow; Zelenskyy reports new limits on Starshield
stories.impact: Peace progress could ease energy and grain prices over time. Canada, a NATO and G7 member, would feel the effects of any change in security arrangements.
stories.now: Witkoff and Kushner met Putin on Thursday; one report put the meeting at about two hours. Kushner said one goal was to win Putin's agreement for European representatives to join talks on regional security, and that Russia and Ukraine have agreed in principle to what would be the largest prisoner exchange of the war. Interfax reported that Putin proposed a joint Russian-Ukrainian humanitarian mission to the front-line city of Kostiantynivka. In Dublin, Zelenskyy told the European Political Community summit that Ukraine had detected new speed restrictions on Starshield, the military satellite service run by Elon Musk's SpaceX, and was asking Washington for the reason. The Abu Dhabi talks ended Wednesday with no agreement on territory or security guarantees.

stories.backstory: Republicans have held both chambers since January 2025, and all 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate were on the ballot. More than 53 million Americans voted early. Tariffs and high gas prices tied to the Iran war weighed on Trump's approval, and recent polls gave Democrats an edge in most key Senate races. Courts also turned back a Trump administration bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots.
stories.headline: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate seat as Hyde-Smith concedes
stories.impact: Canadian exporters are watching whether a Democratic Congress moves to limit tariffs, which could ease pressure on Ontario manufacturers over time; near-term tariffs stay in place unless the White House changes them.
stories.now: CNN's decision desk projected Scott Colom the winner on Wednesday, when the Associated Press count showed him 4,585 votes ahead, and the AP and NBC News followed with their own calls. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith's campaign confirmed she called Colom to concede late Wednesday afternoon, and she said in a video message that she respects the voters' decision. Colom, a district attorney, is the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since 1982 and will be the state's first Black senator since the Reconstruction era after the Civil War. Counties still have until Friday to send official results to the secretary of state. Alaska is now the last uncalled Senate race: Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan 49% to 47.2% in first-choice votes in the latest count, with the ranked-choice tabulation set for Nov. 18.

stories.backstory: Ontario first gave 'strong mayor' powers to Toronto and Ottawa in 2022 and later extended them to dozens of cities. This spring the province brought in the Better Regional Governance Act, letting it appoint chairs in Durham, Halton, Muskoka, Peel, Waterloo and York and the Simcoe warden, and cutting the size of Niagara's council. Some of these posts were previously chosen by voters or by regional councillors. The appointments come right after the Oct. 26 municipal elections.
stories.headline: Ousted Muskoka chair 'deeply disappointed' as backlash to Ford's regional picks grows
stories.impact: For York, Peel, Durham and Halton residents, regional chairs now have more say over budgets that drive property taxes and over approvals for housing and infrastructure. Watch the first regional budgets under the new chairs.
stories.now: Jeff Lehman, who was Muskoka's district chair until the province replaced him with Scott Aitchison, said Wednesday he was deeply disappointed by the decision. In York, Markham Mayor Frank Scarpitti called new chair Steven Del Duca, who stays on as Vaughan's mayor, deeply conflicted and no friend of Markham, and said the job gives one person overriding power over nine mayors and a roughly $5.2-billion regional budget. Del Duca said he will speak for all nine York municipalities and that none can be left behind. Municipal Affairs Minister Rob Flack rejected claims the picks are party insiders, noting Del Duca once led the Ontario Liberals; the other appointees are Kevin Ashe (Durham), Ann Mulvale (Halton), Frank Campion (Niagara), Nando Iannicca (Peel), Scott Davey (Waterloo) and Don McIsaac as Simcoe County warden. The chairs can hire or fire senior staff, veto some bylaws and propose the regional budget, and their term starts Nov. 15. Durham's new chair, Pickering Mayor Kevin Ashe, told CBC he is considering using the expanded powers on the regional budget, and Ontario New Democrat MPP Jeff Burch said the appointments undermine local democracy.

stories.backstory: A federal public inquiry found that China was the most active foreign state trying to interfere in Canada's democratic institutions. Relations soured for years over arrests, tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles and Chinese duties on Canadian canola. Carney's government has since sought to rebuild trade ties with Beijing as tariffs from the Trump administration hit Canadian exports, which drew a tariff threat from Trump over any Canada-China deal.
stories.headline: Carney tells Dublin summit Canada has a part in Europe's security guarantees
stories.impact: GTA residents with family or business ties to China are among those most exposed to interference concerns. Any trade easing could matter for Ontario exporters and for car buyers, while friction with the U.S. over China ties could complicate Canada-U.S. trade talks.
stories.now: Speaking in French as the summit opened, Carney said security guarantees for Ukraine are a European responsibility that also involves Canada and the United States. He was due to hear from Ukraine's president in the afternoon on the state of talks with Russia, and had meetings scheduled with the prime ministers of Greece and Cyprus. Carney framed the visit as part of drawing Canada closer to the European Union to open business opportunities; Canada is the only non-European country invited. From Ireland he travels to Manila to meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Saturday, then to Cambodia and the APEC leaders' meeting in Shenzhen on Nov. 18–19, where he plans to raise foreign interference with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

stories.backstory: Democrats won both chambers of Congress on Nov. 3 and take control in January, which gives their committee chairs subpoena power for the first time in Trump's second term. Garcia said before the election that officials could face subpoenas on day one. Oversight of the executive branch is a routine function of Congress, though administrations of both parties have resisted it.
stories.headline: Garcia says Democrats 'not going to be deterred' by White House warning on probes
stories.impact: There is no direct effect on Ontario, but a Washington consumed by investigations may have less room for trade deals, and probes could touch tariff and minerals decisions that matter to Canadian exporters.
stories.now: Garcia told NPR on Thursday that Democrats will not be deterred or intimidated and that Congress has wide latitude to investigate the executive branch. The Hill reported that he has also warned White House chief of staff Stephen Miller to preserve documents. White House counsel Will Scharf's letter, dated Nov. 9 and made public Wednesday, accused Democrats of abusive threats and said efforts to intimidate officials through congressional proceedings could cross into criminality. The Washington Post reported that the counsel's office has added 15 lawyers to prepare for investigations. Democrats have signalled probes of White House construction projects including the ballroom, the Trump family's role in mineral deals and its cryptocurrency dealings.

stories.backstory: Canada has used remission and relief measures to soften the cost of counter-tariffs on its own importers. A recent Finance Canada report found Ottawa approved about $5.6 billion in relief against a projected $2.2 billion, with more than 800 requests still unresolved.
stories.headline: Canada's U.S. envoy warns tariffs are raising costs and chilling investment
stories.impact: Schools and some public bodies in Ontario may face lower costs on imported goods. Businesses importing affected goods may be able to apply for relief.
stories.now: Mark Wiseman, Canada's ambassador in Washington, told CNBC on Wednesday that uncertainty over tariffs is raising the cost of investing and putting companies off expanding, including in the United States. The federal government extended its tariff relief program beyond U.S. steel imports, so goods used by public education bodies, including those mandated by Indigenous organizations, can also qualify; Newsweek reports the program now runs to June 30, 2028, while exemptions are being withdrawn for some U.S. goods where Canadian alternatives exist. On Tuesday, Carney said the Trump administration remains the main authority on trade agreements even after Democrats won Congress, and Ottawa will keep working toward a deal that suits Canada. Democrats have pledged to try to repeal tariffs on Canada, but they would need Republican votes to override a veto. Trump has also threatened new tariffs on Canadian vehicles starting in January.

stories.backstory: The bank cut its key rate to 2.25% in October 2025 as tariffs slowed the economy. Energy prices then surged with the Iran war, and annual inflation reached 3.1% in September, although core measures stayed near 2%. On Oct. 28 the bank raised its rate a quarter point to 2.5%, its first hike in about three years, and said further increases might be needed.
stories.headline: Bank of Canada notes show oil shock drove its October rate hike
stories.impact: GTA homeowners with variable-rate mortgages or renewing soon should watch Dec. 9. If oil keeps falling, pressure for another increase may ease; if it rebounds, borrowing costs could rise again.
stories.now: The Bank of Canada published its summary of Governing Council talks on Tuesday afternoon. Members considered two options, holding the policy rate at 2.25% or raising it to 2.5%, and the main reason they hiked was that oil prices tied to the Middle East war were expected to stay elevated. They also judged that stronger growth would use up spare capacity in the economy and that rising business costs would eventually show up in core inflation. Since the decision, Brent crude has fallen roughly 20% from its late-October peak, which could ease that worry. The next rate decision is Dec. 9.

stories.headline: Israeli strike on Gaza's Nasser Hospital kills six, including a surgeon
stories.summary: Gaza health authorities say an Israeli airstrike hit the surgical wing of Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis early Thursday, killing six people; Israel says it targeted a Hamas commander.
stories.now: The Gaza Health Ministry said the dead include a 52-year-old general surgeon, Rizk Abu Shaira, and a 13-year-old boy; counts of the wounded range from about 20 to 28. Hospital director Ahmed al-Farra said the strike halted surgeries and stopped work in the radiology department and laboratory. Israel's military said it struck the commander of Hamas's Khan Younis Brigade, whom it named as Muhammad Abu Ismail, and other militants; it did not provide evidence. One report said it was the seventh time the hospital complex has been hit since the war began. Haaretz reported at least 10 people killed in Israeli strikes across Gaza on Thursday.
stories.backstory: The war began with the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and Israel's military campaign has since destroyed much of Gaza's health system. Nasser Hospital is one of the few large medical facilities still working in the territory. A U.S.-backed ceasefire took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, but Israeli strikes have continued, with each side accusing the other of violations. Hospitals are protected under international humanitarian law unless they are used for military purposes.

stories.impact: There is no direct effect on daily life in Ontario. The war remains a deeply felt issue for many GTA communities and has prompted protests and heightened security in Toronto.

stories.headline: Inquest opens into 2020 Peel police shooting of Jamal Francique
stories.summary: A coroner's inquest began Thursday into the death of Jamal Francique, who was shot in the head by a Peel Regional Police officer during an attempted arrest in Mississauga nearly seven years ago.
stories.now: The inquest is expected to run 11 days and hear from nine witnesses. Francique was shot on Jan. 7, 2020, and died in hospital two days later. Ontario's police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit (SIU), said officers had been investigating him over alleged drug dealing and gun possession but could not confirm those allegations and moved to arrest him for allegedly breaching bail conditions. Jurors cannot assign blame or legal liability, but they can recommend changes meant to prevent similar deaths.
stories.backstory: In January 2021 the SIU found no reasonable grounds to charge the officer who fired. Francique's family disputed that conclusion, and their lawyer said the report had several deficiencies. The family sued police, paramedics, the SIU and others in June 2022. The province announced the inquest in November 2025; it is mandatory under Ontario's Coroners Act.

stories.impact: Peel Regional Police serve about 1.5 million people in Mississauga and Brampton, so any recommendations on arrests, use of force or emergency care would affect policing there. The findings are not binding, but police services are expected to respond to them.

stories.headline: Ottawa says Russian players will be barred from world juniors, even with visas
stories.summary: The federal government said Wednesday that Russian and Belarusian athletes will not be allowed into Canada to play in the world junior hockey championship in Alberta, despite a sports court ruling that Russia must be reinstated.
stories.now: Adam van Koeverden, the secretary of state for sport, said the immigration minister will assess athletes and officials individually and stop Russians and Belarusians from entering Canada to compete, whether or not they already hold valid visas. The government said its position will not change while Russia's war in Ukraine continues. Norway's hockey federation said the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had told it Russia would take Norway's place in the tournament in Edmonton and Red Deer. Federations including Finland, Sweden, Czechia and Norway have said their teams will refuse to play against Russia. Hockey Canada said it backs the government.
stories.backstory: The IIHF has kept Russia and Belarus out of most international competition since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Late last month the Court of Arbitration for Sport, the top tribunal for international sports disputes, ordered the IIHF to admit Russian teams to five upcoming championships, starting with the world juniors. The IIHF said it disagreed with the ruling. Canada hosts this year's tournament, which begins in late December.

stories.impact: The world juniors are a holiday-season fixture for hockey fans in Ontario. The decision makes it likely the tournament goes ahead without Russia, though the final lineup is still unsettled.

stories.backstory: Massie's articles centre on the Iran war, which he says has run more than 90 days without approval from Congress, and also cite operations in Venezuela and Yemen. He first filed them in the fall, but the House left early for the campaign. Democrats won the House in the Nov. 3 midterms and take control in January; their leader Hakeem Jeffries calls himself a hard yes on impeachment.
stories.headline: Absent Democrats let Hegseth impeachment die; House GOP picks Jim Jordan as leader
stories.impact: The effects for Ontario are indirect: fights over the Iran war and Pentagon policy can shape oil prices and U.S. defence and trade priorities. Watch for how a divided Washington handles tariffs and Canada talks.
stories.now: The House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to send Rep. Thomas Massie's eight impeachment articles to the Judiciary Committee, ending the effort for this Congress. Eleven Democrats were absent; had all voted no, the motion would have failed 215-211. Several, including Reps. Melanie Stansbury, Marilyn Strickland and Jonathan Jackson, blamed traffic and a police escort near the Capitol, while Nancy Pelosi had flown to San Francisco for a Veterans Day event and others cited medical or personal reasons; colleagues criticized the absences on Wednesday. Trump said the effort had failed miserably. Also Tuesday, House Republicans elected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio as their leader for the next Congress, 106-73 over Majority Leader Steve Scalise, after Speaker Mike Johnson declined to seek the post.
